summary.text: The ninth term is an explicit counterexample: the product of the first nine primes is \(223092870\), giving \(49770428644836901\), which is divisible by \(29^2\). Since \(29\) is not a unit, this term is not squarefree, so the conjunction fails regardless of the infinitude claim.

full_proof.text:
Let \(p_0=2,p_1=3,p_2=5,\ldots\) denote the primes in increasing order, and put
\[
P_n=\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}p_k,
\qquad
a(n)=P_n^2+1.
\]
Thus \(P_n\) is the product of the first \(n\) primes; in particular the empty product gives \(P_0=1\) and \(a(0)=2\), in agreement with the indexing of the sequence.

Recall that a positive integer is squarefree if no square \(d^2\), with \(d>1\), divides it. Equivalently, no prime occurs to exponent at least two in its prime factorization. We will show that \(a(9)\) is not squarefree by exhibiting the square \(29^2\) as a divisor.

The first nine primes are
\[
2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_9
 &=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13\cdot17\cdot19\cdot23\\
 &=223{,}092{,}870.
\end{aligned}
\]
It follows directly from the definition that
\[
a(9)=223{,}092{,}870^2+1
     =49{,}770{,}428{,}644{,}836{,}901.
\]

We now test this number modulo \(29^2=841\). The primorial has the exact division
\[
223{,}092{,}870=841\cdot265{,}270+800.
\]
Hence
\[
P_9\equiv800\pmod{841}.
\]
Moreover,
\[
800^2+1=640{,}001=841\cdot761.
\]
Therefore
\[
a(9)=P_9^2+1\equiv800^2+1\equiv0\pmod{841}.
\]
Thus
\[
29^2=841\mid a(9).
\]
For completeness, the corresponding exact integer identity is
\[
49{,}770{,}428{,}644{,}836{,}901
 =841\cdot59{,}180{,}057{,}841{,}661.
\]
Since \(29>1\), this is already a nontrivial square divisor, so \(a(9)\) is not squarefree. In fact, \(29\) is prime: any proper prime divisor of \(29\) would be at most \(\sqrt{29}<6\), while none of \(2,3,5\) divides \(29\). Thus the displayed divisibility may also be viewed as a repeated prime factor \(29^2\) in \(a(9)\).

Now consider the proposed combined assertion
\[
\bigl(\forall n\in\mathbb N,\ a(n)\text{ is squarefree}\bigr)
\quad\text{and}\quad
\bigl(\text{there are infinitely many }n\text{ for which }a(n)\text{ is prime}\bigr).
\]
If this conjunction were true, its first part would imply, on taking \(n=9\), that \(a(9)\) is squarefree. The divisor \(29^2\mid a(9)\) with \(29>1\) contradicts that conclusion. Hence the first part of the conjunction is false, and therefore the conjunction itself is false. This counterexample does not need to decide the separate question of whether infinitely many terms are prime.
